purpose: Warfarin helps prevent dangerous blood clots from forming or getting bigger in your blood vessels. It is used for conditions like atrial fibrillation (an irregular heartbeat), deep vein thrombosis (clots in the legs), pulmonary embolism (clots in the lungs), and in people with certain heart valve problems. Keeping your blood from clotting too easily helps lower your risk of stroke and other serious problems.
how_it_works: Your body uses Vitamin K to make proteins that help your blood clot. Warfarin works by blocking how your body uses Vitamin K, which makes it harder for clots to form. Think of it like turning down the dial on your blood's clotting ability so it flows more freely and safely.
common_side_effects: The most common concern is bleeding, which can show up as easy bruising, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, heavier menstrual periods, or blood in your urine or stool. You might also notice cuts taking longer than usual to stop bleeding. Let your doctor know if you see pink, red, or dark brown urine, or red or black tarry stools, as these can be signs of more serious bleeding.
warnings: This medication can cause serious or life-threatening bleeding, so it is very important to take it exactly as prescribed. Many foods — especially leafy green vegetables like spinach, kale, and broccoli — and other medications including aspirin, ibuprofen, and many herbal supplements can change how warfarin works in your body. You will need regular blood tests called INR checks to make sure your dose is right. Avoid activities that could cause injury, and always tell every healthcare provider, including your dentist, that you are taking warfarin before any procedure.
typical_dosing: Warfarin is taken by mouth once a day, usually at the same time each evening. Your dose is very personal — it is carefully adjusted based on your regular blood test results (called INR or PT tests). A common starting dose is between 2 mg and 5 mg per day, but your doctor will fine-tune this just for you. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your healthcare provider first.
